title: The Three Best Arguments Against a Knowledge Rich Curriculum
author: Jon Hutchinson
source: Jon's Substack (jonhutchinson.substack.com), November 7, 2026 (repost of a 2018 essay)
summary: Jon Hutchinson reposts a 2018 essay that steelmans the strongest objections to a knowledge-rich curriculum before rebutting them, framed by a new introduction on why he now writes about belonging. Inspired by Rapoport's Rules for civil disagreement, he tests his own position against the best opposing arguments. The first objection is that children need skills, not knowledge, answered with the cognitive-science point that skills are domain specific and arise from foundational knowledge, so teaching knowledge is how skills are built. The second is that enquiry learning is more natural and motivating, answered with Geary's distinction between biologically primary and secondary knowledge, which implies that hard cultural knowledge needs explicit instruction and not a fingers-crossed approach. The third is that knowledge-rich curricula rob teachers of autonomy, answered by separating intended, implemented and enacted curriculum and placing teacher autonomy in the enacted level, as a surgeon exercises judgment while following a prepared procedure. He closes by inviting counterarguments and rejecting the sneering that often marks debates on his own side.
points: Hutchinson models good-faith disagreement by stating each opposing argument at its strongest, following Rapoport's Rules, before replying.
Against the skills-not-knowledge claim, he argues that skills are domain specific and rest on stored knowledge, so the route to critical thinking is teaching powerful knowledge.
Using Geary's primary versus secondary knowledge, he says enquiry learning suits knowledge that is picked up naturally, while hard cultural knowledge needs explicit, sequenced instruction.
On autonomy, he separates the intended, implemented and enacted curriculum and places teacher freedom in how content is taught, not in building materials from scratch.
A shared, coherent curriculum over years also prevents gaps and repeats, such as children meeting the Vikings four times and never studying African history.
quotes: In the age of social media, it’s easy to enter a debate in bad faith, defaulting to your ‘tribe’ and presuming bad intentions of those who disagree with you. I think that this is not only a pretty depressing worldview, it’s just straightforwardly incorrect.
You can’t directly teach skills; they arise from, and supervene upon, knowledge. And not all knowledge is equal.

Experts who think critically, in the way that we want children to, are in fact doing a huge amount of work under the surface. They effortlessly and unconsciously select, assimilate and compare thousands of facts stored in their long-term memory.

Biologically secondary knowledge is effortful and difficult and our brains are not really designed through evolution to engage in thinking in this way. As a result, even with a good enquiry question, we will often opt out of thinking about the hardest stuff, allow others to carry the cognitive load, or simply be unaware of what it is we are supposed to be learning.

Essentially, the enquiry model in most cases is what I call the ‘fingers crossed’ approach. Maybe they will stumble across lots of knowledge, and understand it, and construct amazing ideas that stick for life. But maybe they won’t.

It is not necessary to write a powerpoint on the Romans, or a story about the Battle of Hastings, or a diagram of the water cycle, or multiple examples of direct speech being punctuated correctly (or incorrectly) to exercise autonomy in delivering these lessons.
Teachers should have autonomy, but this should be placed almost entirely in the enacted level of the curriculum.
Rather than robbing teachers of their autonomy, then, these knowledge rich approaches actually unleash teachers and allow them to exercise it where it really matters.
